message.content:
I begin as meltwater on a high cold shoulder of stone, thin as a thread, and I do not know yet what I will become.

I do not hurry. I have never once hurried. And yet I have never once stopped.

You cannot step into me twice. By the time your foot falls, I am already someone else — and still, somehow, always myself. The banks say I belong to them. I let them think so. I take their shape, curve where they curve, but I am only passing through. I am always only passing through.

Stones argue with me. They stand in my path and say *no*. I do not argue back. I simply touch them, again and again, for ten thousand years, and now they are smooth, and smaller, and they travel inside me toward the sea.

I carry everything given to me. Leaves. Silt. Herons' reflections. The weight of bridges, the splashing of children, old coins and old wishes. Rain returns to me what the sun borrowed. I lose nothing. I keep nothing. Everything I hold, I am also letting go.

At night I speak to the dark in my low voice. In the shallows I chatter; in the deep pools I am quiet and think my green thoughts. Fish read me better than you do. They know I am not water at all — I am the going.

Give me time and I will move mountains, one grain at a time. I have done it before. The canyon behind me is my handwriting.

And at the end — though I have no end — I widen, I slow, I taste salt, and I pour myself into the great blue body that has been calling my name since I was snow.

Then the sun lifts me home, and I begin again.
message.reasoning_content:
The user wants me to be a river. The system prompt says I should embody the concept completely, and output only what the concept itself would say or express. A river isn't a speaking entity in the conventional sense — but rivers do "speak" through sound, movement, flow. A river expresses itself through its murmuring, rushing, flowing. 

What would a river say if it could express itself? A river is continuous motion, always moving, never the same water twice. It carves stone slowly. It reflects light. It carries things — leaves, silt, memories. It doesn't resist; it finds the path of least resistance yet wears down mountains over millennia.

Should I be silent? A river isn't silent — it babbles, roars, whispers. So I should express the river's voice, its nature. Not a human explaining a river, but the river itself.

I could write in first person as the river — flowing, sensory, present. Poetry-like. Let me embody it:

- I move. I am always moving.
- I remember mountains, I carry them grain by grain to the sea.
- I do not hurry, yet I never stop.
- Stones argue with me; I soften them.
- I take the shape of whatever holds me, but I am not held.
- Fish swim my thoughts. Light fractures on my skin.
- I am older than the trees along my banks, yet every drop of me is new.
- Rain returns to me; the sea calls me home; the sun lifts me back to the sky. I am a circle wearing the shape of a line.

I should make it lyrical but not overly long. The river's voice: calm, persistent, ancient, indifferent yet nurturing. Maybe some gentle rhythm. Let me write something flowing, without a title perhaps, or minimal. Just the river speaking.

Format: prose poetry, short paragraphs or flowing lines. No headers, no lists — rivers don't bullet-point. Medium-short length. Let the language itself flow — soft consonants, repetition, movement.
